title: Who Framed Roger Rabbit
wiki_lead:
Who Framed Roger Rabbit is a 1988 American fantasy comedy film directed by Robert Zemeckis and written by Jeffrey Price and Peter S. Seaman, based on Gary K. Wolf's 1982 novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit? It combines live action and animation and is set in a world in which humans and cartoons co-exist. Bob Hoskins stars as Eddie Valiant, a private investigator in Hollywood in 1947, who must help exonerate Roger Rabbit (voiced by Charles Fleischer), a cartoon rabbit who has been framed for murder. Christopher Lloyd, Stubby Kaye and Joanna Cassidy co-star.
Walt Disney Studios purchased the film rights to the novel shortly after its publication. Price and Seaman wrote two drafts of the script before Disney brought in executive producer Steven Spielberg and his production company, Amblin Entertainment. Zemeckis was brought on to direct and Canadian-British animator Richard Williams was hired to supervise the animation sequences. Production was moved from Los Angeles to Elstree Studios in England to accommodate Williams and his animators. While filming, the production budget rapidly expanded and the shooting schedule overran.
Who Framed Roger Rabbit was released through Disney's Touchstone Pictures banner in the United States on June 22, 1988. It received acclaim for its visuals, humor, writing, performances and groundbreaking combination of live-action and animation. It grossed $351.5 million worldwide, becoming the second-highest-grossing film of 1988, behind Rain Man. It renewed interest in the golden age of American animation, spearheading the renaissance age of American animation and the Disney Renaissance. It won three Academy Awards for Best Film Editing, Best Sound Effects Editing and Best Visual Effects and received a Special Achievement Academy Award for Williams' animation direction. In 2016, Who Framed Roger Rabbit was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant".

Plot
In 1947 Los Angeles, animated cartoon characters, or "toons", co-exist with humans. Private detective Eddie Valiant, once a staunch ally of the toons, has become a depressed alcoholic following his brother Teddy's murder by an unknown toon five years prior. Maroon Cartoon Studios owner R.K. Maroon, upset about the recent poor performance of his toon star Roger Rabbit, hires Eddie to investigate rumors that Roger's glamorous toon wife, Jessica, is having an affair with Marvin Acme, owner of the Acme Corporation and Toontown, the animated metropolis in which toons reside.
After watching Jessica perform at The Ink and Paint Club, Eddie secretly photographs her and Acme playing patty-cake. He shows the pictures to Roger, who becomes distraught, refusing to believe Jessica was unfaithful. The next morning, Acme is found murdered, and evidence implicates Roger. grok_lead: Who Framed Roger Rabbit is a 1988 American live-action/animated fantasy comedy film directed by Robert Zemeckis and starring Bob Hoskins as private detective Eddie Valiant. Loosely adapted from Gary K. Wolf's 1981 novel Who Censored Roger Rabbit?, the story is set in a 1947 version of Los Angeles where anthropomorphic cartoon characters called "Toons" coexist with humans as second-class citizens. Valiant reluctantly takes on the case of clearing Toon star Roger Rabbit âvoiced by Charles Fleischer âof murdering Acme Pictures owner Marvin Acme, uncovering a conspiracy involving Toon Town's future and the sinister Judge Doom played by Christopher Lloyd. The film features extensive cameos by iconic cartoon figures from Warner Bros., Disney, and other studios, blending their exaggerated physics with real-world environments. Produced by Amblin Entertainment with executive producer Steven Spielberg, the $70 million production employed hand-drawn animation composited over live-action footage captured on VistaVision film, using mechanical rigs, puppeteers, and optical printing to achieve seamless interactions without relying on computer-generated imagery. This technical feat adhered to strict rules ensuring Toons cast realistic shadows, respected props, and followed live-action lighting while amplifying cartoonish behaviors, setting a benchmark for hybrid filmmaking. Released by Touchstone Pictures, it earned $351 million worldwide, ranking as the second-highest-grossing film of 1988, and secured three Academy Awards for Visual Effects, Film Editing, and Sound Editing. The film's success revitalized interest in traditional animation and influenced subsequent Toon-human crossover projects, though its dark noir elements and violence prompted debates over its PG rating suitability.
